head.h1: Holi Catering in Dubai — Menus, Prices and What's Included

opening_paragraph: Holi catering in Dubai from myCHEF is live chaat counters, cooling thandai and festival sweets at your venue, from AED 700 per person. A vetted chef cooks on site and keeps the counters running through the day. The festival of colour is loud, joyful and made to be enjoyed hands-free, so we take the whole food operation off your plate: menu design, on-site cooking, service and a full clear-down. You throw the gulal; we keep the counters flowing. Tell us your date, guest count and venue, we typically reply within 15 minutes during business hours, with an itemised proposal to follow you can plan around.

new_paragraphs: How much does holi catering cost in Dubai?

It starts from around AED 700 per person and is quoted by guest count, menu and service level. Buffet and drop-off are the most economical; live stations and plated service sit higher. Send your numbers for an itemised quote.
What's included in holi catering?

Menu design, a vetted chef cooking on site, service staff where needed, plating, setup and full cleanup. In short, the whole food operation is handled so you can enjoy the colours instead of the kitchen.
How far ahead should I book?

A week is usually enough for a small gathering; book earlier for large parties and peak festival dates. Popular Holi weekends fill quickly, so the sooner you share your date the better we can hold your chef.
Can you make the Holi menu vegetarian, vegan or Jain?

Yes — a holi menu in Dubai is naturally vegetarian-friendly, and we build fully vegan or Jain spreads, plus gluten-free and nut-free options, with allergens labelled at every counter so guests choose with confidence.
Do you cater corporate Holi parties and large events?

Yes — corporate holi catering in Dubai is one of our busiest formats, covering offices, community events and villa parties. We scale stations and staff to the headcount while keeping food fast, fresh and cooked to order.
Is the food kept colour-safe, away from the gulal?

Yes — live stations are positioned away from the colour play, food is served covered and to order, and staff manage hygiene so guests move cleanly between the gulal and the counters throughout the party.
Which areas of Dubai do you cover for Holi catering?

We cover all of Dubai, from Jumeirah, Palm Jumeirah and Emirates Hills villas to apartments and offices in Business Bay, Downtown and Dubai Marina. If you are searching for holi catering near me, we most likely reach you.
For holi catering, the chefs and partner kitchens handling your booking operate to Dubai Municipality food-safety requirements .

add_block.new_heading: Holi party styling, colour-safe logistics and dietary care
new_paragraphs: Great Holi food is as much about logistics as flavour, because colour and catering have to share the same space safely. We position live stations away from the gulal zone, serve food covered and to order, and station staff to manage hygiene so guests move cleanly from the colour play to the counters. Timing matters too: chaat and fried snacks are cooked in waves so they arrive crisp, not sitting under heat lamps. On the styling side, we lean into the festival's palette — bright serviceware, marigold and colour-block table dressing, and counters that look as photogenic as the celebration itself. Dietary care runs through all of it: because Holi menus are plant-forward by nature, most of the spread already suits vegetarian and vegan guests, and we label every allergen so nobody has to ask twice.

add_block.new_heading: Can we celebrate Holi in Dubai?
new_paragraphs: Holi is widely marked in Dubai. The practical constraint is where rather than whether, and it is a venue question: confirm with the building, community or venue what they permit on coloured powder before you plan the day, because policies differ and are set locally.

For catering it changes two things. Food is served away from the colour, under cover, because powder travels further than anyone expects. And the menu leans to items that survive being eaten standing up with colour-stained hands — chaat, tikka, stuffed breads and sealed sweets rather than a plated course.
